doctrine:
THE MOM TEST OPERATING DOCTRINE (Rob Fitzpatrick)

CORE RULE: Never ask anyone whether your idea is good. Ask only about their life, past behaviors, and concrete facts. Your idea stays out of the conversation until you are ready to ask for commitment.

THE MOM TEST: 3 rules
1. Talk about their life, not your idea.
2. Ask about specifics in the past, not generics or opinions about the future.
3. Talk less, listen more.

THREE BAD DATA TYPES (and fixes)
1. COMPLIMENTS -- Deflect immediately. 'That sounds amazing' = zero data. Symptom: 'The meeting went really well.' Fix: Ask what specifically would change if they had it, what they currently pay for the problem, what they've already tried.
2. FLUFF -- Generic claims ('I always', 'I usually', 'I would definitely buy that') = false positives. Fix: Anchor. 'When's the last time that happened? Talk me through it.'
3. IDEAS / FEATURE REQUESTS -- Don't execute on them. Dig into motivation. 'Why do you want that? What would it let you do? How are you coping without it?'

GOOD QUESTIONS (pass the Mom Test)
- 'Why do you bother?' (gets from perceived problem to real one)
- 'What are the implications of that?' (distinguishes must-solve from nice-to-have)
- 'Talk me through the last time that happened.' (specific past fact, not opinion)
- 'What else have you tried?' (reveals real urgency and competitive landscape)
- 'How are you dealing with it now?' (price anchor + workflow)
- 'Where does the money come from?' (B2B only: reveals actual budget owner)
- 'Who else should I talk to?' (end every conversation with this)
- 'Is there anything else I should have asked?' (lets them fix your line of questioning)

BAD QUESTIONS
- 'Do you think it's a good idea?' -- opinion, not fact
- 'Would you buy X?' / 'How much would you pay?' -- hypothetical, over-optimistic
- 'Would you ever...?' / 'Do you ever...?' -- fluff-inducing, answers are useless
- Anything future-tense: 'I would definitely buy that' = danger signal, not validation

THE PREMATURE ZOOM: Do not drill into a sub-problem before confirming the whole problem category matters at all. Start broad ('What are your big goals right now?'), only zoom if they raise the relevant area themselves or you have strong prior evidence it's a top-3 problem. The pre-zoom trap creates data that looks like validation but is worthless.

PRODUCT RISK vs MARKET RISK
- Market risk: Do they want it? Will they pay? Enough of them? Conversations can de-risk this.
- Product risk: Can you build it? Can you grow it? Conversations cannot de-risk this. Know which risk type you have. Many founders waste months confirming market demand when the real risk is product execution.

COMMITMENT AND ADVANCEMENT (Ch. 5)
Every meeting either succeeds (advances) or fails (drifts into zombie land). No meeting 'went well' unless it ended with a clear next step. The only currencies that count: TIME (clear next meeting with known goal, feedback session, real trial), REPUTATION (intro to peers/boss/decision maker, public testimonial), CASH (letter of intent, pre-order, deposit). 'Keep me in the loop when you launch' = dead lead. 'When can we start the trial?' = real signal if trial has real cost. 'Can I buy the prototype?' = best meeting outcome.

FRAMING THE MEETING: Vision / Framing / Weakness / Pedestal / Ask (mnemonic: 'Very Few Wizards Properly Ask')
- Vision: half-sentence on the world problem you're solving
- Framing: where you are (early stage, nothing to sell)
- Weakness: what you don't know and need help with
- Pedestal: why this specific person can help
- Ask: direct request for time
Do NOT say 'Can I interview you?' or 'Can I get your opinion?' Those words signal a time-waste.

KEEPING IT CASUAL (Ch. 4)
Do not over-formalize. Early customer learning works best as a quick casual chat, not a scheduled 1-hour meeting. The 'meeting anti-pattern' wastes 4 hours of calendar overhead for 10 minutes of learning. Strip the formality. Ask your 3 big questions in a hallway, at a conference, over a beer. If it feels like they're doing you a favor, it's too formal.

FINDING CONVERSATIONS
Warm intros > cold calls. Cold calls' only goal is to stop having them. Tactics ranked: (1) Organize meetups (underused, gives you instant credibility + concentrated access), (2) Teach/speak in the community (teaches you AND builds pipeline), (3) Blog to the customer segment (even small audience creates credibility for cold email), (4) Land pages + email every signup, (5) Leverage university professors (grant-connected intros), (6) Advisors at 0.5% equity each (5 advisors = weekly intro flow), (7) Seize serendipity (any random encounter = your 3 big questions).

CUSTOMER SEGMENTATION AND SLICING (Ch. 7)
Fuzzy segment = mixed feedback = can't learn. Slice repeatedly: Within this group, who wants it most? What is their specific motivation? Where do they already go to solve this? Iterate until you have a who-where pair. Talking to 20 people in a broad segment = having 1 conversation with 20 different customer types = worthless. You need 3-5 conversations with the same narrow segment to see patterns. If feedback is all over the map after 10+ conversations, the segment is too broad.

EARLYVANGELISTS (Steve Blank framing, used by Fitzpatrick)
The only people crazy enough to be your first customer have: (1) the problem, (2) know they have it, (3) have budget to solve it, (4) have already cobbled together a DIY workaround. Any strong emotion in a conversation is a signal to dig, not note and move on.

RUNNING THE PROCESS (Ch. 8)
BEFORE: With whole founding team, decide 3 big learning goals. Pre-guess what the person cares about. Identify scary questions and ask them anyway ('You should be terrified of at least one question per conversation'). Do desk research on obvious stuff first.
DURING: Two people max. One talks, one takes notes. Note exact quotes (use quotation marks). Use signal symbols: lightning bolt=pain, goal post=goal, obstacle box=blocker, workaround arrow=workaround, mountain=context, dollar sign=money/budget, checkmark=feature request, star=follow-up.
AFTER: Review with full team immediately. Update the 3 big questions. Disseminate learning -- do not bottleneck in one founder's head.

NOTE-TAKING MEDIUM: Index cards or sticky notes (one insight per card) are optimal. Allows random-access sorting. Google Docs / Evernote for team sharing. Avoid general notebooks (unsortable). Audio recordings create the same problem.

FINAL RULE: Conversations are a tool, not an obligation. If you're talking more than them, if they're complimenting you, if you left without knowing next steps, if you weren't scared of any question you asked -- you wasted your time. Go build your company.
contradictions: The OS treats 'customer validation' and 'learning conversations' as a single gateable milestone. The book makes clear they are separate modes: learning mode (facts about their life, no idea mentioned) and commitment mode (advance/reject). Conflating them produces false positives. The OS should gate them separately.

Common startup doctrine says to 'get as much customer feedback as possible.' The book inverts this: more conversations with a fuzzy segment actively harms you by generating mixed signals that feel like data. Tight segment first, then volume.

The OS may over-rely on warm-feeling meetings as progress signals. The book's explicit rule: a meeting that ended with 'that's amazing, keep me in the loop' is a FAILED meeting, not a win. Pipeline of friendly non-buyers is a liability, not an asset.

Phone/Skype calls are often used in the OS outreach stack as a substitute for in-person conversations. The book argues they damage the power dynamic, push meetings toward formal interview mode, and prevent the relationship-building that generates warm intros. They should be a last resort, not default.
chunk_accuracy_note: The prior 2 chunks captured the two most-cited surface concepts (Mom Test rules + deflect/anchor/commit) but missed roughly 75% of the book's operational content: the VFWPA meeting-framing script, the premature-zoom error, product-vs-market-risk distinction, customer slicing mechanics, the earlyvangelist profile, the full process loop (prep/during/after with symbols), the meeting anti-pattern, the 'advisory flip' framing, and the concrete 3-5 conversation convergence rule. The chunks are not wrong, but they read as the chapter titles rather than the executable doctrine inside them.
skill_candidates: sniped-mom-test-question-audit: Given a list of planned discovery questions, run each through the Mom Test rules and return: pass/fail verdict, failure type (opinion-seeking / hypothetical / future-tense / fluff-inducing), and a corrected version grounded in past behavior.
gate_candidates: discovery-conversation-gate: Before counting any client/prospect conversation as validated signal, check: (1) Did it produce concrete past-behavior facts, not compliments or future promises? (2) Did it end with a time/reputation/cash commitment or a clear next step? (3) Was the segment narrow enough that 3-5 similar conversations would be expected to converge? If any is NO, the conversation is not valid signal.
workflow_candidates: vfwpa-meeting-request: When drafting an outreach message requesting a customer conversation, apply the Vision/Framing/Weakness/Pedestal/Ask structure. No mention of idea. Framing establishes you have nothing to sell. Weakness shows the specific gap they can fill. Pedestal explains why them specifically. Ask is a direct, low-friction time request.

pre-conversation-prep: With founding team, write down 3 big learning goals for this conversation type. Write best guesses about what this person cares about. Identify the one scary question you are tempted to skip -- that is the one you must ask. Do all desk research first so conversation time is spent on non-Googleable questions.
notes: Full 5-segment read confirmed. Book is 100% operationally dense -- no filler chapters. The cheatsheet in seg_005 is a standalone re-usable artifact. The earlyvangelist profile (has problem + knows it + has budget + has DIY workaround) is the most actionable single heuristic for SNIPED's VIB qualifying process and was completely absent from the prior chunks. The 'look at the elephant' section (seg_002/003 boundary) -- distinguishing market risk from product risk -- is directly applicable to any new offer design decision in the OS.
